articles.summary: Impact of Native American Scholarship Program Reflected in Past, Current Recipients mboyle Tue, 11/03/2026 - 08:01 Post Image November 3, 2026 - As Native American Heritage Month begins, Freeport is recognizing students who have used our Native American Scholarship Program to pursue educational and professional opportunities in their communities and beyond. Among them are two recipients at very different points in their careers: one just beginning her education with hopes of serving Native American communities through healthcare, and another now working as a nurse in the UK. Working with partners like Education Forward Arizona, Freeport helps create educational opportunities in the communities in which the company operates. Through the Native American Scholarship Program, eligible students can receive financial support as they pursue higher education. “For more than a decade, our Native American Scholarship Programs have opened doors that many of our students once thought were out of reach,” said Ondrea Barber, Manager-Global Indigenous Affairs & Human Rights. “With over $7 million invested and more than 550 scholarships awarded, we’ve helped Native American students become nurses, engineers, teachers and leaders who are giving back to their own communities and making a positive impact on the world.” Among the more recent recipients is Maureen Ford. A member of the Navajo Nation, Ford is a junior at Emory University in Atlanta and a recipient of the 2026-2027 Native American scholarship. Pursuing a bachelor's degree in human health, Ford hopes to one day build a career in healthcare leadership through organizations such as the Indian Health Service or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Passionate about improving healthcare access, strengthening public health programs and increasing Native American representation in health data and research, Ford plans to earn a Master of Public Health after completing her undergraduate studies and is considering medical school. She said a strong foundation in public health can create opportunities to improve health outcomes in Native communities and beyond. And Ford isn't alone when it comes to advancing the health of communities – whether it's those we're born into or the ones we eventually come to call home. For Shasha Tenijieth, the daughter of a Freeport employee and a member of both the San Carlos Apache and White Mountain Apache tribes, the Native American Scholarship Program helped support an educational journey that stretched far beyond Arizona. Finding scholarships that would support a student attending university outside the United States wasn’t always easy, Tenijieth said. Through the Native American Scholarship Program, however, she was able to pursue a degree in pediatric nursing and even complete an elective placement in East Africa before graduating from the University of Salford in the United Kingdom. She remains there today, where she now works as a pediatric cardiac nurse. Looking back, Tenijieth said the scholarship provided more than financial assistance. “The scholarship opened doors for me,” Tenijieth said. “Programs like Freeport’s relieve a lot of the financial stress and allow students to focus on their studies. Thanks to that, I had the opportunity to follow my passions, study internationally and build a career doing what I love.” Photos (top to bottom): A junior at Emory University, Maureen Ford hopes to one day have a career with Indian Health Service or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; After attending college in the UK, Shasha Tenijieth now lives and works there as a pediatric cardiac nurse.
articles.title: Impact of Native American Scholarship Program Reflected in Past, Current Recipients

articles.summary: Honoring Veterans: USS Arizona to Carry Freeport Copper mboyle Wed, 11/11/2026 - 08:07 Post Image November 11, 2026 - Copper from Freeport mines in Arizona is being used to cast the bells that will adorn the new United States submarine being built bearing the vaunted name USS Arizona. Freeport donated 100 pounds of copper to a group of American Legionnaires, who are using it to cast at least three bells, one of which will be placed on the new submarine expected to be put to sea in the next few years. As the company honors nearly 1,000 employees who have served in the U.S. military this Veterans Day, the Freeport copper aboard the Arizona is a fitting tribute to employees and Arizonans who have helped defend the nation, said Roger Laija, General Manager, Rod and Refining. “It gives me shivers,” said Laija, himself a Navy veteran who has been involved in the bell-casting project and helped arrange the donation. “Every veteran I talk to about this wants to be a part of it – Freeport employee or not. They understand the importance of it. “There’s a lot of tradition with the bells, so being asked to provide copper to produce the alloy to cast bells for the USS Arizona submarine brings a lot of pride. Being a Navy veteran, working in our operations in Arizona and knowing how important bells are in the Navy and what they symbolize, it’s awesome to know that copper from our mines in Arizona is going into bells that will be placed at the port and on the vessel.” A Dark Day in U.S. History The USS Arizona name carries profound historical and emotional significance, honoring the battleship sunk during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. The attack claimed the lives of 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the ship and propelled the United States into World War II. The battleship remains submerged in Pearl Harbor, where more than 900 crew members remain entombed. Today, the USS Arizona Memorial is among the most visited memorial sites in the U.S. The new submarine will be the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name Arizona, a legacy dating back to the Civil War, and the first since the battleship was lost at Pearl Harbor. In December 2019, the Navy announced the name USS Arizona would be revived as a new Virginia-class submarine. The submarine currently is under construction, with commissioning anticipated in 2029, according to the USS Arizona Legacy Foundation, a nonprofit organization that supports the submarine's crew while honoring the legacy of the lost battleship. The casting of the bells from Arizona copper was the idea of Chris Balsley, a Sons of the American Legion member whose job in the conveyor belt industry gave him experience working with mining companies in the state. After the announcement that the Navy would be launching a new USS Arizona, he discussed the idea of casting bells from Arizona copper with fellow Legionnaires. Eventually, the state Legion headquarters established a committee to make the pitch to the Navy. Freeport Copper Working with the legacy foundation, Balsley and the Legion secured Navy approval for the project. They then approached Freeport about donating copper from its Arizona mines and were connected with Laija, who coordinated the donation. The copper came from Freeport’s mines in Morenci, Bagdad and Safford, and was processed through the Miami rod mill. Because pure copper is unsuitable for bells, it was combined with brass grommets from American flags donated to the Legion for disposal. Laija, who does sand casting as a hobby, initially offered to make the bells. However, a Legion member involved in the project is producing them at his home foundry. At least three bells will be made. The Navy will select one for the submarine and another for its home port. Using Arizona copper for the bells is an important connection between the state and those who will defend the nation onboard the submarine, Balsley said. “It does carry a lot of special meaning,” he said. “It holds a lot of symbolism.” Photos (top to bottom): Roger Laija, a Navy veteran, said Freeport’s donation of copper for the USS Arizona bells is a fitting tribute to the state and Arizonans who have served in the military; The flag that flew on the USS Arizona during the attack at Pearl Harbor is on display at the Arizona Capitol Museum; Naval guns on the state capitol grounds in Phoenix represent the beginning and end of World War II in the Pacific. One is from the USS Arizona, sunk at Pearl Harbor in 1941, and the other from the USS Missouri where the Japanese surrendered in 1945.
articles.title: Honoring Veterans: USS Arizona to Carry Freeport Copper
